chapters.text:
That night in the saloon, the railroad boss's men made their play: cards, insults, a gun cleared half out of leather. Tom Beckett ended it without firing — the fast peace, the sheriff called it later, shaking their head.

the sheriff was the first to offer a meal and the news. 'the railroad boss means to take it all,' the sheriff said. 'The water, the grazing, the town. Unless somebody stands up.' Tom Beckett ate slowly. Standing up was a habit.

Tom Beckett rode into Red Mesa at sundown, with a land deed in the saddlebag and dust in every seam. The town had the feel of a held breath — and the reason was posted on every wall: the railroad boss's notice, claiming the valley.

chapters.title: The Claim
chapters.text:
the sheriff dug up the records: the original survey, the territorial seal, the witness — old, afraid, but honest. a land deed matched, link by link. the railroad boss's forgery claim started to look like what it was: desperation.

the sheriff stood with Tom Beckett — and then the blacksmith, and the schoolteacher, and one by one half the town. 'We know Tom Beckett's word,' the sheriff said. It wasn't much. It was everything.

Thursday night they came with fire. The livery burned, and a land deed's copies with it — but Tom Beckett had the original where fire couldn't reach. the railroad boss had played the last card. Friday would tell.

chapters.title: High Noon
chapters.text:
the railroad boss stepped out with two gunmen. 'Last chance,' the railroad boss said. 'Ride out.' Tom Beckett thought of Red Mesa, of the sheriff, of every small place that ever needed one person to stand. 'No,' Tom Beckett said.

Friday noon. The street emptied the way streets do before a storm. Tom Beckett walked it alone — the sheriff had argued, but some walks you take solo. a land deed was in the courthouse. This was about more than paper.

The hearing went ahead anyway, because Tom Beckett insisted on it. Law, not guns. a land deed was examined, the witness testified, the seal was verified. The judge — even the railroad boss's judge — couldn't lie with the whole town watching.

chapters.title: The Drive
chapters.text:
the railroad boss's rustlers hit them at the canyon — the last play of a losing hand. The fight was short and decisive: the town rode together, and together is a word the railroad boss never understood.

The saddle tested them: stampede at midnight, Tom Beckett riding the point with a lantern and a prayer; the river crossing, the sheriff swimming the lead steer; the long dry stretch, sharing the last canteen.

They reached the railhead with the herds and the deed and their heads high. Red Mesa was solvent. Red Mesa was free. Tom Beckett looked back at the dust of the trail and felt the peculiar ache of a job done.

chapters.title: Home Range
chapters.text:
Tom Beckett was offered the sheriff's star, the mayor's office, and three ranches. Tom Beckett took none of them. 'I ride,' Tom Beckett said, which explained everything and nothing, the way true things do.

But Tom Beckett stayed through the winter, helping the sheriff mend fences, teaching the kids to read sign, being — for a while — part of Red Mesa instead of just its defender. It suited them.

a land deed stayed in the courthouse, under glass, with the iron likeness beside it. Proof. Promise. courage at high noon — carved, at the sheriff's insistence, on the frame.

chapters.title: Sundown
chapters.text:
Tom Beckett rides somewhere west, where the map goes blank. There are always more valleys, more villains, more folks needing one person to stand. The frontier doesn't end. It just moves.

the sheriff keeps a room ready, and the kettle on, and the news of Red Mesa in letters. 'Come home when the trail allows,' every letter ends. The trail always allows, eventually.

Spring came, and Tom Beckett rode out with the thaw, a land deed's story told and retold in the saloon. the sheriff watched them go from the porch, and didn't wave — waving is for endings, and this wasn't one.
